newsitem.title: UK: UK PSBR data should not prevent tax cuts-analysts.
newsitem.headline: UK PSBR data should not prevent tax cuts-analysts.

text.p: Britain's unexpectedly high budget deficit in September suggests the government will have difficulty meeting its target for the financial year, but it is unlikely to prevent tax cuts in the November 26 budget.
The September public sector borrowing requirement (PSBR) was 3.41 billion stg compared with market forecasts of 2.7 billion.
"The PSBR at face value is disappointing," said Richard Jeffrey, group economist at Charterhouse. "But the Chancellor will still find scope to reduce taxes by a modest amount in the budget."
He expects cuts in personal sector taxation of two to three billion stg, accompanied by measures elsewhere to offset the loss of revenue.
The Office for National Statistics said the September PSBR was inflated by a 1.2 billion stg interest payment on an index-linked gilt. Privatisation proceeds totalled 997 million stg.
Jonathan Loynes, UK economist at HSBC Markets, said the underlying picture was not so bad, with departmental spending growth low for the second month in a row.
However, spending growth was still trending above the Treasury's forecast of 1.8 percent for the full year, possibly pointing to an overshoot on this side of the accounts.

"On the receipts side, disappointing weakness in income tax brought September receipts in lower than we expected but average growth of 5-1/2 percent in the first half of the year exceeds the Treasury forecast of 5-1/4 percent, suggesting it is still too early to get too concerned about receipts," Loynes added.
He said further spending restraint would be needed in the coming months if the government is to meet its target of 27 billion stg for the full-year PSBR.
Jeffrey was also fairly sanguine about PSBR for the full year. "I think it will respond to improving growth and tax revenue flows will beign to increase appreciably," he said.

Robin Aspinall of National Australia Bank said that while the September PSBR was well above expectations, it was still too early to draw conclusions about the total for the 1996/97 financial year, especially with an election looming.
"But the projections of ever-decreasing deficits thereafter are pure fiction," he said.
The ONS said the cumulative PSBR for April to September was 16.14 billion stg against 20.05 billion in the same 1995 period.
David Philpotts of Schroders said he believed the Treasury was probably still on target to meet its target.
"The downtrend in PSBR excluding privatisation receipts is probably still intact," he said.
